opus-5.5.text:
I think about that interview often, the one Arendt did with Günter Gaus in 1964. He asked whether she wanted her work to have wide influence, and she said, more or less, *no, what matters to me is to understand.* She added that if other people understand in the same sense she has understood, that gives her a feeling of satisfaction, like being at home. That stuck with me because it reverses the usual order of things.

In our field, especially in AI right now, "impact" has become almost the only currency. People ask how many citations a paper has, whether it became a benchmark, whether a company adopted it, whether it went viral on Twitter. Impact gets measured from the outside, by how much you move other people. Understanding is internal. It's the moment when something that was confusing suddenly makes sense to you, when you can see why a method works and not just that it works.

My reading of Arendt is not that impact is bad. It's that if you aim at impact directly, you start optimizing for the wrong thing. You chase what's trendy, you pick problems because they'll be noticed, you write the paper to win the leaderboard rather than to answer a question. Then even when you "succeed," you may not have learned anything. If you aim at understanding, impact sometimes follows as a byproduct, and when it does, it tends to be more durable, because it rests on something real.

For me as a researcher, this is quite practical. Many of the works I'm happiest about started from a simple puzzle. Why does this architecture choice matter? Is this component actually necessary, or have we just been copying it? Do we really understand what visual representations these models learn? Those questions came from curiosity, not from a plan to make a splash. Some of the work ended up being influential, but that wasn't the starting point, and honestly I think it would have been worse if it had been.

There's also something freeing in her attitude. If your goal is impact, you're always anxious, because it depends on other people, on timing, on luck, on hype cycles. If your goal is understanding, you control more of it. You can have a very good day of research even if nobody ever cites what you did, because you now see something more clearly than you did yesterday.

So I'd put it this way: impact is about the world's response to you, and understanding is about your relationship with the problem. In a field moving as fast and as noisily as ours, I think it's worth protecting the second one deliberately, for yourself and for your students, because the environment will push you toward the first one constantly.

r001.rationale: The response says Arendt’s priority was understanding rather than wide influence, and frames understanding as the purpose rather than impact.

r002.rationale: It says impact may follow understanding as a byproduct, but does not explain large-scale resonance developing through successive sharing between people.

r003.rationale: It says Arendt felt satisfaction when others understood as she had, but does not say that sharing her understanding meant they also understood her.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first read that line from Arendt, it hit me quite hard, because it describes the trap that I think a lot of us in AI research fall into without noticing.

The way I understand it: she's saying there are two very different motivations for doing intellectual work. One is wanting to be effective, to have influence, to change the world, to be seen. The other is simply wanting to understand something, to see it clearly, for its own sake. And she's suspicious of the first one. Not because impact is bad in itself, but because once impact becomes the goal, it starts to deform the thinking. You begin to ask "what will land?" instead of "what is true?" And those questions have very different answers.

In our field, the word "impact" is everywhere. Citation counts, paper acceptances, how many people use your model, how many GitHub stars. The incentive structure is almost entirely built around impact. And I don't want to be hypocritical, I've benefited from that system, I care about whether my work is used. But I've also noticed that the projects I'm most proud of, the ones that actually ended up mattering, usually started from a very simple feeling of confusion. Something didn't make sense to me. Why does this architecture work? Why does this representation emerge? I wanted to understand it, and I would have wanted to understand it even if nobody ever cited the result.

Whereas the work that started from "this would be a big result if it worked" tends to be more fragile. It chases the trend. It's often technically fine, but it doesn't have that core of genuine curiosity, and I think readers can feel that.

So for me, Arendt's distinction is a kind of reminder, almost a discipline. Impact, if it comes, should be a side effect of understanding, not the thing you aim at. And this is especially important right now, because the field moves so fast and there's so much noise. If you're optimizing for impact, you'll always be reacting to what's hot. If you're optimizing for understanding, you might be slower, you might look out of step for a while, but you're building something that's actually yours. And strangely, that's often what ends up having the most lasting influence anyway.

r001.rationale: The candidate says understanding is pursued “for its own sake” and that impact should be a side effect, communicating understanding as the purpose rather than impact.

r002.rationale: The candidate says understanding may lead to lasting influence, but does not explain resonance growing through successive sharing between people.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that people who share Arendt’s understanding of a problem thereby understand her to some extent.

astra-6.text:
I understand it as a distinction between trying to produce a particular effect on people and trying to see something more clearly. If your starting point is impact, you’re already asking, “How do I get people to think or act differently?” If your starting point is understanding, you have to leave open the possibility that you’re the one who needs to change your mind.

That resonates with how I think about research. We want our work to matter, of course. But if we begin with the demand that every project must have a huge impact, we can end up choosing the conclusion before we’ve really explored the question. Understanding requires a little more patience—and a willingness to discover that your original framing was wrong.

I don’t see those two things as incompatible. Understanding can have a profound impact. The distinction, for me, is what guides the work: are you trying to arrive at an intended effect, or are you willing to follow the question somewhere you didn’t expect?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pursuing an intended effect with seeking understanding, but does not say that understanding itself was the purpose of Arendt’s work.

r002.rationale: It says understanding can have a profound impact, but does not describe resonance growing through successive sharing between people.

r003.rationale: It does not say that people who come to share Arendt’s understanding of a problem thereby understand her.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is about what guides your work. Are you trying to produce a particular effect on the world, or are you trying to understand something—and willing to let what you discover change your mind?

If impact becomes the goal from the beginning, you can start choosing questions because they attract attention, or interpreting results to support the story you want to tell. Understanding requires a different attitude. You have to leave room for an answer you didn’t expect, even one that makes your original question look wrong.

In research, I find that distinction useful. Of course I want my work to matter. But impact is partly outside my control. What I can take responsibility for is whether the question is meaningful, whether the evidence supports the claim, and whether I’ve actually learned something. Understanding can lead to impact, but I wouldn’t treat the two as interchangeable.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding as a goal distinct from impact, but does not say that understanding itself was the purpose of Arendt’s work.

r002.rationale: It does not describe understanding spreading through successive sharing or developing into broad resonance.

r003.rationale: It does not say that people who share Arendt’s understanding of a problem thereby understand her.
